frictionVectors.title: EU Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains dependent on Algerian gas while pressing for market and regulatory access. Algiers is using supply diversification to preserve policy autonomy and resist external political conditionality.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Border Instability
frictionVectors.details: Instability in Mali, Niger, and Libya increases pressure on Algeria's southern borders and energy infrastructure. Foreign military competition in the Sahel complicates Algiers's preference for non-intervention and regional mediation.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Strategic Logistics
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting substantial US, European, and Gulf interest because of its access to critical minerals. Infrastructure investment could improve diversification but also deepen external leverage over transport and export routes.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Debt and Oil Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Angola has reduced some Chinese financing dependence, but oil-linked obligations and foreign participation remain embedded in major infrastructure and energy projects. Declining production heightens pressure to trade future resource value for immediate capital.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Trade Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Political relations with Niger have disrupted established trade and transit patterns through the Port of Cotonou. Benin is seeking alternative commercial partnerships while remaining exposed to decisions made by larger regional powers.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence and militant infiltration threaten northern communities, transport corridors, and prospective resource areas. External security assistance is increasingly important, creating dependence risks alongside the need for rapid capacity building.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is pressing for a larger share of diamond value and greater control over marketing and downstream activity. The dispute tests whether foreign commercial expertise can remain compatible with stronger national ownership.

frictionVectors.title: Resource Diversification Risk
frictionVectors.details: New coal, copper, uranium, and battery-mineral prospects could reduce diamond dependence but may invite uneven foreign concessions. Botswana's regulatory credibility gives it leverage, though limited domestic processing capacity remains a constraint.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The junta's security partnership with Russia-linked forces expands alternatives to Western assistance but creates new political, financial, and operational dependencies. Persistent militant attacks limit the state's ability to secure mines, roads, and rural production.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Sector Nationalization
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are tightening control over industrial mining, artisanal production, and gold marketing to capture more national revenue. The policy may improve sovereign control, but opaque contracting, sanctions exposure, and insecurity could deter investment and encourage smuggling.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking greater state control and value addition in nickel and other mineral projects, but limited capital and processing capacity leave it dependent on foreign investors.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Strained relations with Rwanda and armed-group activity in eastern DRC increase security costs and constrain Burundi's ability to manage cross-border trade and resources independently.

highlights: Tourism and aid shape sovereignty margins

frictionVectors.title: External control of logistics
frictionVectors.details: Port, airport, maritime-security, and digital infrastructure rely heavily on European, Chinese, and other external capital, creating leverage over a strategically located Atlantic state.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism concentration risk
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-owned tourism and transport networks capture a significant share of value, leaving Cabo Verde exposed to external shocks despite strong domestic institutions.

highlights: Oil and timber remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Resource-sector concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and opaque intermediaries retain substantial influence over oil, forestry, mining, and major infrastructure, while weak oversight limits domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and northern insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest, alongside insurgency in the Far North, disrupts transport corridors and reduces effective state control over local resources.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and diamond concessions
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security actors and foreign commercial networks continue to benefit from access to extractive sites, while regulatory capacity and transparency remain weak.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Central African Republic depends on insecure routes through Cameroon and neighboring states for fuel, trade, and humanitarian supplies, limiting sovereign control over infrastructure and supply chains.

highlights: Oil revenue remains the sovereignty anchor

frictionVectors.title: Foreign security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's security posture remains shaped by external military, financial, and diplomatic partners, even as the government seeks greater autonomy after shifts in its relationship with France.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and regional corridor exposure
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline and export revenues are central to state finances, but production, transit infrastructure, and border trade remain vulnerable to foreign operators and instability linked to Sudan and the wider Sahel.

frictionVectors.title: French Control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France's administration of Mayotte remains the central sovereignty dispute, limiting Comoros' control over its claimed territory and maritime space.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on foreign financing, remittances, and external partners for ports, energy, and basic infrastructure, constraining policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and Regional Intervention
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east continues to undermine state control, with Rwanda-linked security accusations, regional involvement, and contested mineral corridors shaping sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and Copper Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese mining dominance and growing Western competition for critical minerals create investment opportunities but leave the state struggling to capture full value and enforce contracts.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil revenues remain central to state finances, exposing Congo to external price cycles and limiting diversification of sovereign economic power.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, rail, and port projects expand connectivity but raise concerns over debt exposure, contract transparency, and long-term control of strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Revenue Imbalance
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is strengthening domestic processing and regulation, but foreign buyers and global commodity pricing still capture much of the cocoa value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Expansion of Abidjan's port and transport links increases regional leverage while intensifying competition among French, Chinese, Turkish, and Gulf-backed investors.

frictionVectors.title: Base and Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its location through foreign military bases and port concessions, but overlapping external interests constrain independent control of strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Ethiopian Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains tightly tied to Ethiopia's trade access and to Chinese-financed infrastructure, creating leverage but also exposure to debt, political, and regional-security shocks.

frictionVectors.title: IMF AND GULF CAPITAL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: External financing and Gulf investment support Egypt’s balance of payments but increase foreign influence over strategic assets and economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: NILE DAM DISPUTE
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam continues to threaten Egypt’s long-term water security.

highlights: Gas strategy seeks a second wind

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON DECLINE
frictionVectors.details: Maturing fields and limited diversification are reducing state revenues, leaving the government exposed to foreign operators, market volatility, and declining production.

frictionVectors.title: OPAQUE RESOURCE GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: Weak transparency around oil, gas, and infrastructure contracts limits domestic oversight and increases the risk that external commercial interests capture disproportionate value.

frictionVectors.title: RED SEA POWER COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea’s coastline and proximity to maritime chokepoints attract regional interest, while tensions with Ethiopia and wider Red Sea insecurity constrain sovereign maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: MINING PARTNERSHIP DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Copper, zinc, and gold revenues rely heavily on foreign technical and financial partners, creating exposure to commodity cycles and contractual disputes.

frictionVectors.title: SACU AND SOUTH AFRICAN DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal stability depends heavily on customs revenues and economic access through South Africa, limiting Eswatini’s autonomy during regional downturns.

frictionVectors.title: WATER AND AGRICULTURAL CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Large agricultural and industrial projects compete with domestic water needs, while external investors retain significant influence over land-intensive production.

frictionVectors.title: NILE DIPLOMACY
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam expands Ethiopia’s control over electricity generation but continues to generate acute strategic friction with Egypt and Sudan.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL FINANCE AND INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, Chinese infrastructure exposure, and Gulf and Turkish investment provide essential capital while constraining policy space amid internal conflict and fiscal stress.

highlights: Manganese and oil remain strategic anchors

frictionVectors.title: Contract and concession uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are pressing for greater state participation and local processing in oil, manganese, and timber, creating tension with established foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Budget pressures and infrastructure needs keep Gabon reliant on international lenders and foreign investors, limiting the autonomy of its resource-nationalist agenda.

highlights: Senegal remains the key strategic partner

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia depends heavily on foreign capital and regional transit links to modernize Banjul, leaving strategic infrastructure exposed to competing external interests.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore resource uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Potential offshore hydrocarbons attract outside exploration interest, but limited state capacity and unresolved maritime considerations constrain effective sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and environmental loss
frictionVectors.details: Unregulated gold mining, including activity linked to foreign and domestic networks, damages water systems and undermines the state's control over extraction and revenue.

frictionVectors.title: External financing leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed fiscal reforms and creditor negotiations constrain policy space, while Ghana seeks more local processing and stronger state participation in gold, lithium, and oil.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou foreign consortium leverage
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore and rail-port system is dominated by large international partners, making Guinea's export future dependent on complex external financing, logistics, and offtake arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite concentration risk
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators retain a central role in bauxite extraction and export, while the military government faces pressure to increase state control without disrupting vital revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign traders and processors capture much of the value from Guinea-Bissau's dominant cashew sector, while weak infrastructure limits domestic processing and bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Port and illicit-network vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Bissau's limited maritime enforcement and political instability create openings for transnational trafficking networks and external influence over strategic port activity.

highlights: Port and corridor sovereignty under pressure

frictionVectors.title: Strategic infrastructure financing
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is seeking to diversify infrastructure and development financing beyond traditional Chinese and Western partners. Debt-service pressures limit Nairobi's bargaining room over ports, railways, energy, and logistics assets.

frictionVectors.title: Regional corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Competition among Mombasa, Lamu, and alternative regional corridors creates pressure over transport concessions and security commitments. Instability in neighboring states also raises the cost of protecting cross-border infrastructure.

highlights: Water remains the core sovereign asset

frictionVectors.title: Water-export dependency
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports to South Africa provide essential revenue but leave the country structurally dependent on Pretoria for pricing, infrastructure, and market access. The next phases of the Lesotho Highlands Water Project increase both fiscal opportunity and negotiating exposure.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Diamond production is exposed to volatile prices, foreign ownership, and limited domestic processing capacity. The government has leverage through licensing but remains dependent on external capital and technical expertise.

highlights: Concessions drive growth but limit capture

frictionVectors.title: Iron-ore concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron-ore operations and proposed expansions can generate jobs and export revenue, but foreign operators retain substantial control over capital, logistics, and marketing. Weak domestic processing leaves Liberia exposed to commodity cycles and limited value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics influence
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port is central to Liberia's fiscal and commercial sovereignty, with external investors and partners influential in modernization and operations. Concession terms and customs capacity remain sensitive issues.

frictionVectors.title: Competing oil authorities
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security networks continue to contest control over oil facilities, revenue flows, and key appointments. This fragmentation weakens the state's ability to negotiate consistently with international energy companies.

frictionVectors.title: External military and commercial leverage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign governments, security contractors, and regional networks retain influence over bases, transport routes, and energy infrastructure. Their involvement complicates efforts to establish unified national control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependency
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, graphite, and other mineral projects depend heavily on foreign capital, technology, and export markets. Madagascar gains foreign exchange but remains vulnerable to price shocks, contract asymmetry, and limited domestic refining.

frictionVectors.title: Land and conservation disputes
frictionVectors.details: Mining, infrastructure, and agribusiness expansion regularly generate tensions over land rights, local consultation, and environmental protection. Conservation finance and foreign development partners can also constrain domestic policy space when project conditions are contested.

highlights: Mining ambitions meet governance and infrastructure gaps

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Prospective uranium, graphite and rare-earth projects attract foreign capital, but Malawi has limited leverage over financing, processing and offtake terms.

frictionVectors.title: Power and transport dependence
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and dependence on regional corridors weaken sovereign control over industrial development and increase reliance on external lenders.

highlights: Junta tightens control over gold sector
Russian security ties deepen strategic dependence

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector confrontation
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is asserting greater state participation and revenue capture from industrial mining, creating friction with foreign operators and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Security-for-access alignment
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security support expands the junta's room for maneuver but risks opaque resource arrangements and reduced Western financing.

highlights: Gas production opens a new fiscal chapter
Nouakchott balances Gulf, European and Chinese capital

frictionVectors.title: Offshore gas governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project can strengthen state revenues, but foreign operators, cross-border Senegalese coordination and local-content demands test Mauritania's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and corridor concentration
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore exports and new green-hydrogen ambitions depend heavily on foreign infrastructure, finance and export corridors, limiting domestic value capture.

highlights: Indian Ocean sovereignty remains strategically sensitive

frictionVectors.title: Chagos sovereignty settlement
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's claim over the Chagos Archipelago remains tied to negotiations over the Diego Garcia military facility and wider Indian Ocean security interests.

frictionVectors.title: External finance and maritime exposure
frictionVectors.details: The economy benefits from international investment and logistics links but remains vulnerable to external shocks, shipping disruptions and regulatory pressure from larger partners.

highlights: Western Sahara remains the core sovereignty front

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate, fisheries and renewable-energy projects in the territory generate legal and diplomatic challenges, despite expanding international support for Morocco's autonomy proposal.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is building domestic renewables, ports and manufacturing capacity, but still relies on imported hydrocarbons, foreign technology and external markets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mozambique relies on foreign and regional forces to contain the Cabo Delgado insurgency around strategic gas infrastructure. This limits state control over the security environment surrounding resource assets.

frictionVectors.title: LNG Contract Leverage
frictionVectors.details: International energy firms retain substantial influence over project timing, financing, and revenue structures. A production restart could strengthen state finances while preserving significant external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: New offshore discoveries are increasing competition among international operators for licenses and infrastructure access. Namibia is seeking stronger local benefits without deterring the capital and technology required for development.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Energy Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Green hydrogen and port projects depend heavily on external financing, engineering, and export markets. This creates long-term risks of infrastructure and value-chain dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Border Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Oil exports and mining logistics depend on corridors exposed to insurgent violence, sanctions pressure, and political friction with neighbors. Limited transport alternatives reduce Niger's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Shifting External Patrons
frictionVectors.details: The authorities are reducing French influence while expanding ties with Russia, Turkey, and other non-Western partners. This may increase diplomatic autonomy but risks replacing one form of external dependence with another.

highlights: Refining Capacity Could Reduce Import Exposure
Oil Theft Still Erodes State Control

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Oil-Contract Leverage
frictionVectors.details: International firms remain central to upstream investment, technology, and financing even as Nigeria seeks more domestic participation. Contract disputes and regulatory uncertainty continue to weaken the state's negotiating position.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Port Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Oil theft, sabotage, and maritime insecurity reduce public revenue and raise operating costs. Dependence on private and foreign-linked security and logistics providers complicates sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Allegations
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda faces persistent international scrutiny over alleged support networks connected to mineral flows from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. The dispute threatens sanctions exposure, regional trade, and Kigali's diplomatic room.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Technology Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's development model relies on external aid, investment, and imported digital and infrastructure systems. Strong state coordination improves bargaining capacity but does not eliminate dependence on outside capital and markets.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore oil uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Exploration in the Joint Development Zone with Nigeria remains a potential revenue source, but weak commercial certainty and limited state capacity constrain São Tomé and Príncipe's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, aviation, and energy upgrades depend heavily on foreign finance and contractors, leaving the archipelago exposed to competing Portuguese, Chinese, and other external interests.

frictionVectors.title: Contract renegotiation pressure
frictionVectors.details: The Faye administration is seeking greater state participation and transparency in oil and gas projects, creating friction with international operators and lenders over contract stability.

frictionVectors.title: Gas infrastructure and revenue risk
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim and Sangomar developments can strengthen fiscal sovereignty, but cost overruns, production delays, and revenue-management weaknesses remain significant risks.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime security competition
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles relies on external partners, particularly India and other maritime powers, for surveillance and patrol capacity across its large EEZ, creating recurring sensitivity over strategic access.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Heavy dependence on tourism and imported infrastructure leaves the country vulnerable to external financing conditions, climate shocks, and foreign control of strategic facilities.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mining corridors
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mineral projects remain dependent on foreign operators and logistics networks linking mines to railways and ports, limiting domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt leverage
frictionVectors.details: Expansion around Freetown and Pepel requires external capital, while debt and fiscal pressures can force concessions that weaken long-term control over transport infrastructure and natural resources.

frictionVectors.title: Turkey-linked energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Somalia's offshore exploration partnership with Turkey could unlock petroleum resources, but security, financing, and revenue-sharing arrangements may give Ankara substantial leverage over emerging energy assets.

frictionVectors.title: Ports, territory, and security rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Competing Turkish, Emirati, Ethiopian, and other external interests around ports and Somaliland intersect with federal-state disputes and al-Shabaab's insurgency, weakening unified Somali control of strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Competition for Minerals
frictionVectors.details: South Africa retains regulatory control over platinum-group metals, manganese, and chromium, but competing Western, Chinese, and Gulf investors are seeking greater influence over processing and supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Freight Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity unreliability and weak rail and port performance reduce the state's ability to capture value from mining and strengthen dependence on private and external infrastructure capital.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil exports remain dependent on transit infrastructure and refining access through Sudan, leaving sovereign revenue exposed to conflict, shutdowns, and external bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: Elite and Foreign Resource Capture
frictionVectors.details: Political elites, neighboring states, and external oil firms compete for control of production and payments while weak institutions limit transparent national management of resource income.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and External Patrons
frictionVectors.details: Competing armed authorities and foreign networks seek access to Sudanese gold, while Gulf, Russian, Egyptian, and regional interests shape trade routes and military supply channels.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Oil Corridor Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Conflict threatens Port Sudan and the infrastructure linking oil-producing areas to export routes, increasing leverage for whichever faction controls transport and customs nodes.

frictionVectors.title: External Control of Logistics
frictionVectors.details: Expansion of ports, railways, and logistics corridors is attracting Chinese, Gulf, Indian, and Western capital, creating opportunities while raising concerns about long-term concession and debt leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Value-Chain Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The government is pursuing greater local processing of graphite, nickel, and other minerals, but foreign firms retain substantial financing, technology, and market power.

frictionVectors.title: Port Dependence and External Finance
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's strategic port role strengthens Togo's regional leverage but leaves customs revenue and logistics resilience sensitive to foreign operators, lenders, and shifting coastal security conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate Processing Gap
frictionVectors.details: Togo retains control of its phosphate resource base but captures limited downstream value, creating continued dependence on external capital, technology, and commodity markets.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains constrained by limited access to international financing and difficult negotiations with the IMF, increasing reliance on European support and bilateral partners. This reduces policy space while fiscal pressure limits investment in strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Migration-for-Support Leverage
frictionVectors.details: The EU and individual European states continue to link financial and political cooperation to migration management. Tunisia seeks sovereign control over border policy, while European pressure creates a persistent asymmetry in the relationship.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Environmental Conflict
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline remains central to Kampala's export strategy but faces sustained legal, environmental, and investor pressure from European institutions and civil society groups. Delays or financing constraints could weaken Uganda's control over the timing and value of its petroleum development.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign lenders have financed major transport and energy projects, strengthening connectivity but increasing repayment exposure. Uganda retains policy autonomy, yet debt-service demands may encourage resource-backed or concession-based arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Copper Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking greater domestic processing, tax capture, and transparency from multinational copper operators while competing for capital from Chinese, Western, and Gulf-linked investors. The country remains vulnerable to external price cycles and limited bargaining power over technology and downstream markets.

frictionVectors.title: Power Shortages Threaten Mining Expansion
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower shortfalls and drought-related generation problems constrain copper output and industrial growth. Emergency imports and new generation projects can stabilize supply, but they also deepen dependence on regional power markets and external capital.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is using export restrictions and beneficiation requirements to capture more value from lithium and other strategic minerals, but Chinese and other foreign firms still provide much of the capital, technology, and market access. The resulting tension limits how far Harare can impose sovereign control without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions, Currency, and Mining Finance
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions and Zimbabwe's unstable monetary environment complicate access to banking, equipment, and long-term project finance. This pushes the mining sector toward alternative financiers and trading networks, increasing opacity and bargaining risks around gold and other resources.
